title: Count of Beautiful Arrangements
hints: rather than generating a full permutation and checking it afterward, check the divisibility condition the moment you place each number - invalid placements can be pruned immediately
recurse by position, from 1 to n; at each position, try every still-unused value from 1 to n
only recurse into a value if it satisfies value % position == 0 or position % value == 0 - skip it entirely otherwise, without recursing

mark a value used before recursing to the next position, count a completed arrangement once position exceeds n, and unmark the value (undo) after that branch returns so the next candidate value can be tried at this position
commonMistakes: generating full permutations first and validating afterward instead of pruning during construction, which is correct but far slower
checking the condition with the wrong index (0-indexed position instead of the 1-indexed position the problem defines it against)
forgetting to unmark a value as unused after backtracking out of a branch, which silently makes some numbers permanently unavailable

content.problemStatement:
You're given an integer `n`. Consider arrangements (permutations) of the numbers 1 through n placed into positions 1 through n. An arrangement is called beautiful if, for every position `i`, either the number placed at position `i` is evenly divisible by `i`, or `i` is evenly divisible by the number placed at position `i`.

**Count how many beautiful arrangements exist.**
constraints: positions and values are both 1 to n, 1-indexed
at position i, the placed value v must satisfy v % i == 0 or i % v == 0
notes: n = 2 (smallest case with more than one arrangement)
a larger n to confirm the count is computed correctly, not just estimated

optimal.time: O(k) for some k substantially smaller than n!, since invalid branches are pruned as early as position 1 instead of being fully built out
optimal.space: O(n) for the used-values tracker and recursion depth
optimal.pattern: backtracking that fills positions 1 to n in order, only trying values that satisfy the divisibility condition at the current position, with a used-values tracker

bruteForce.approach: generate all n! permutations of 1..n and check the divisibility condition at every position for each one
